question: Has road safety for pedestrians in Brooklyn gotten better since 2013? Make a chart suitable for a local news story and summarize the findings.

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians injured and killed, shown separately
options.grouping: Brooklyn crash year and pedestrian outcome (injured/killed)
options.reason: Separate annual injury and death counts show the human toll without allowing the much smaller fatality count to disappear on a shared scale.
options.answer: This file cannot establish whether walking risk fell, but recorded Brooklyn pedestrian injuries fell 22.1% (3,641 to 2,835) while deaths rose 30.0% (30 to 39), a mixed change in the recorded toll.
options.interpretation: This answers whether the annual pedestrian toll has improved: injuries declined from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, while deaths rose from 30 to 39. Separate count series are a defensible way to show both outcomes without combining injury and death severity. It does not measure risk per pedestrian trip or population because the file has no walking-exposure denominator. It uses full Brooklyn years 2013–2025; 0 of 473,801 selected rows (0.0%) lack either pedestrian count, 0 of 506,806 Brooklyn rows (0.0%) have NULL crash dates and cannot be assigned to a year, and 691,375 of 2,269,187 file rows (30.5%) have NULL borough and cannot be assigned to Brooklyn; partial 2012 and 2026 are excluded, so no partial year is included.

options.metric: Brooklyn crash reports with at least one pedestrian injured or killed
options.denominator: All Brooklyn police-reported crash records in the same calendar year
options.reason: The share of Brooklyn crash reports involving pedestrian harm distinguishes the frequency of harmful crashes from changes in the overall volume of crash reports.
options.answer: This file cannot establish whether walking risk fell, but the share of Brooklyn crash reports involving pedestrian injury or death rose from 7.4% in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025 (53.0% higher relative).
options.interpretation: This answers whether pedestrian-harm crashes became less common relative to all reported Brooklyn crashes: their share rose from 7.4% in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025. This denominator is defensible for comparing how often Brooklyn crash reports involve pedestrian harm despite changes in total crash-report volume. It leaves unanswered the risk per walking trip or population, because pedestrian exposure is not in the file. It uses full Brooklyn years 2013–2025; 0 of 473,801 selected rows (0.0%) lack either pedestrian count, 0 of 506,806 Brooklyn rows (0.0%) have NULL crash dates and cannot be assigned to a year, and 691,375 of 2,269,187 file rows (30.5%) have NULL borough and cannot be assigned to Brooklyn; partial 2012 and 2026 are excluded, so no partial year is included.

answer:
The crash counts show mixed change from 2013 to 2025: Brooklyn pedestrian injuries fell 22.1%, from 3,641 to 2,835, while deaths rose 30.0%, from 30 to 39; the data cannot establish whether risk per walking trip fell.
Pedestrian harm appeared in a larger share of Brooklyn crash reports in 2025 than in 2013—11.4% versus 7.4%—but this crash-based measure cannot establish whether risk per walking trip fell.
